sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: The category "vegetable" is culinary, not botanical — it includes leaves, stems, roots, flowers, seeds, and fruits from dozens of unrelated plant families. But within this diversity, a few genera demonstrate extraordinary breadth: *Brassica oleracea* produced seven distinct crops from a single wild ancestor through selective breeding. The story of vegetables is a master class in how artificial selection can sculpt plant form.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
WHAT WE CALL "VEGETABLE" — BOTANICAL DIVERSITY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Part selected    Example                     Family
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Leaf             Spinach, lettuce, chard     Amaranthaceae, Asteraceae
Stem             Asparagus, kohlrabi         Asparagaceae, Brassicaceae
Root             Carrot, parsnip, beet       Apiaceae, Amaranthaceae
Tuber            Potato, yam                 Solanaceae, Dioscoreaceae
Flower bud       Broccoli, cauliflower       Brassicaceae
Fruit (culinary) Tomato, pepper, cucumber    Solanaceae, Cucurbitaceae
Seed             Peas, beans                 Fabaceae
Bulb             Onion, garlic               Amaryllidaceae

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
There is no unified botanical definition of "vegetable."
It is purely a culinary/cultural category.

sections.text: ## Brassica oleracea: One Ancestor, Seven Crops

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: This is the most remarkable case of artificial selection in plants. *Brassica oleracea* is a wild coastal plant from the Atlantic European coastline — a modest, mustard-family plant. Every following crop was created by selecting different plant parts for development.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
BRASSICA OLERACEA WILD ANCESTOR
Mediterranean/Atlantic coast plant
Unremarkable mustard-family herb
Biennial: year 1 = vegetative; year 2 = flowers/seeds

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
B. oleracea (wild)
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          │                    │                    │
   SELECT terminal      SELECT axillary      SELECT stem
   leaf bud             buds                (internode)
          │                    │                    │
     CABBAGE             BRUSSELS               KOHLRABI
   (tight head of        SPROUTS               (swollen stem,
    modified             (small heads           not root)
    leaves)              on stem)
          │
   Further modification:
     Leaf surface:    → KALE (open leaves, no head)
     Leaf curliness:  → COLLARD GREENS (flat kale)
     Flower clusters: → BROCCOLI (immature flower heads)
     Flower clusters
     (abnormal):      → CAULIFLOWER (dense white, albino)
     Cauliflower
     (variant):       → ROMANESCO (fractal geometry —
                                   Fibonacci spiral florets)
```

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: All are the same species (*Brassica oleracea*) and are interfertile — they can cross-pollinate. This is why open-pollinated brassicas can produce bizarre hybrids in the garden.

sections.text: ### Nutritional Properties

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: Brassicas are rich in glucosinolates — sulfur-containing compounds that give them their characteristic pungency. When cells are disrupted:

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
GLUCOSINOLATE HYDROLYSIS
Intact cell: glucosinolate (stored in vacuole) + myrosinase (stored in cell)
Cell damaged (cutting, chewing):
  glucosinolate + myrosinase + water → isothiocyanates + glucose + sulfate

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
Products include:
  Sulforaphane (broccoli): induces phase 2 detoxification enzymes,
    associated with cancer-risk reduction in epidemiological studies
  Allyl isothiocyanate: mustard oil pungency
  Erucin: similar structure to sulforaphane

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
KEY: myrosinase is denatured by heat → cooked broccoli has less
     sulforaphane unless gut bacteria compensate (they partially do)
     Raw broccoli > cooked broccoli for sulforaphane activity
```

sections.text: ## Solanaceae: The Nightshade Family

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: The Solanaceae are a dramatic example of parallel domestication across the Americas. Four unrelated crops from one family, each domesticated independently in different regions.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
MAJOR SOLANACEAE CROPS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Taxon           Crop      Origin        Domestication    Wild ancestor
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
S. lycopersicum Tomato    Andes/Mexico  ~3,500 BP        S. pimpinellifolium
                                                         (small red cherry)
S. tuberosum    Potato    Andes         ~8,000 BP        Multiple Solanum spp.
S. melongena    Eggplant  S/SE Asia     ~2,500 BP        S. insanum (spiny)
S. quitoense    Naranjilla Ecuador/     limited           wild
                          Peru
Capsicum spp.   Peppers   Mexico        ~6,000 BP        Multiple Capsicum spp.
                                                         (see spices/06)
Physalis        Tomatillo Mexico        pre-Columbian    Wild Physalis
peruviana       Cape gooseberry
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
All share: alkaloids (tomatine, solanine), similar floral structure,
           5-merous flowers, berry fruits botanically
```

sections.text: ### The Alkaloid Issue

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: All Solanaceae contain some level of alkaloid compounds as herbivore deterrents.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
SOLANACEAE ALKALOIDS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Solanine (potato): concentrated in green skin, sprouts, unripe parts
  Toxic threshold: ~2-5 mg/kg body weight
  Green potato: up to 200 mg/100g (dangerous)
  Normal potato flesh: <10 mg/100g (safe)
  Mechanism: cholinesterase inhibitor (same as nerve agents, but far milder)

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
Tomatine (tomato): present in unripe tomatoes + leaves
  Ripe tomato: very low levels, effectively non-toxic
  Green tomato: higher but still low; culinary use is traditional

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
Capsaicin (pepper): technically not a "solanine" alkaloid but alkaloid-related
  Does not harm most mammals at food doses
  See spices/06 for full treatment

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
HISTORICAL FEAR: When tomatoes/potatoes arrived in Europe (~1500s),
  they were correctly identified as nightshade relatives
  (Deadly nightshade = Atropa belladonna) → refused for 100+ years
  The fear was not irrational — the plant family includes true toxins
```

sections.text: ### Tomato: From Wild Cherry to Modern Cultivar

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
TOMATO DOMESTICATION AND DEVELOPMENT
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Wild ancestor: S. pimpinellifolium — 1cm red cherries, Peru/Ecuador
~3,500 BP: Mexican/Central American selection → larger fruit
1519: Hernán Cortés sees tomatoes in Aztec markets → sent to Spain
~1520-1550: Italy introduces "pomo d'oro" (golden apple) — likely yellow var.
~1550-1600: Grown in Italy, Spain; used medicinally; eaten by poor
~1700-1800: Gradual uptake in Southern Italy (Neapolitan poor eat it)
1820: Robert Johnson eats tomato on Salem NJ courthouse steps
       to prove it's not poisonous (story disputed)
1860s: Transcontinental US = tomato mainstream
1893: US Supreme Court rules tomato is vegetable for tariff purposes
       (Nix v. Hedden: "tomato" = vegetable in commerce, fruit in botany)
1994: Flavr Savr tomato — first GM food approved for sale
       (antisense polygalacturonase → slower softening)
       Commercial failure (didn't taste better + GMO stigma)
```

sections.text: ## Allium: The Chemistry of Sharpness

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: The genus *Allium* (family Amaryllidaceae) includes ~900 species, ~20 of which are cultivated food crops. All share the characteristic sulfur-based volatiles that give them pungency.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

```
MAJOR ALLIUM CROPS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Species            Common name    Origin          Notes
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. cepa            Onion          Central Asia    Most widely cultivated
A. cepa var.       Shallot        Central Asia    Cluster of small bulbs
  aggregatum
A. cepa var.       Scallion       Various         Non-bulbing form
  proliferum
A. sativum         Garlic         Central Asia    Multiple cloves, propagated
                                                  clonally (rarely seeds)
A. ampeloprasum    Leek           Mediterranean   Elongated, mild
A. ampeloprasum    Elephant       Mediterranean   Very large, mild
  var. ampeloprasum  garlic
A. schoenoprasum   Chives         Northern        Fine flavor, leaves used

sections.text: ### The Thiosulfinate Chemistry

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
ALLIUM PUNGENCY MECHANISM
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INTACT CELL:
  Precursor: alliin / S-allylcysteine sulfoxide stored in the vacuole
  Enzyme: alliinase stored in the cytoplasm — PHYSICALLY SEPARATED

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
CELL DAMAGED (cutting, crushing):
  Alliin + alliinase → allicin + other thiosulfinates

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
ALLICIN (diallyl thiosulfinate):
  The principal fresh garlic compound
  Highly unstable: breaks down within hours to:
    Diallyl disulfide (main cooked garlic compound)
    Diallyl sulfide, ajoene (long-term fermentation products)
  Not present in cooked garlic (heat destroys alliinase)

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
ONION TEARING:
  Propanethial S-oxide gas released by LF-synthase enzyme
  Diffuses to eye mucous membranes → reacts with water → sulfenic acid
  Sulfenic acid → propanethial S-oxide → irritates
  Prevent: chill onion (slower enzyme), cut under water, wear goggles

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
PRACTICAL:
  Raw garlic: allicin (sharp, antibacterial)
  Cooked garlic: diallyl disulfide + other compounds (sweet, mellow)
  Aged black garlic: allicin converted to S-allylcysteine (antioxidant)
  Garlic powder: no allicin (heating during drying destroys alliinase)
```

sections.text: ## Cucurbitaceae: Gourd Family

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, zucchini, melons, watermelons — all cucurbits. Some of the earliest domesticated plants.

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
KEY CUCURBITS AND ORIGINS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Cucumis sativus (cucumber): India, ~3,000 BP
Cucumis melo (melon, cantaloupe, honeydew): Africa/India, ~4,000 BP
Citrullus lanatus (watermelon): Sub-Saharan Africa, ~5,000 BP
  Wild ancestor: bitter; cultivated for water in desert
Cucurbita pepo (pumpkin, zucchini, acorn squash): Mexico, ~10,000 BP
  One of the "Three Sisters" with maize and beans
Cucurbita maxima (butternut squash, Hubbard): S. America, ~4,000 BP
Cucurbita moschata (butternut): Mexico/Central America
Lagenaria siceraria (bottle gourd): ANOMALY
  African origin, but found in Asia and Americas pre-Columbian
  Floated across oceans? Carried by early humans? Mystery solved?
  DNA evidence (2014): bottle gourd reached Americas ~10,000 BP —
  from Africa via Atlantic (not Asia via Pacific); first plant known
  to cross Atlantic independently before humans
```

sections.text: ## Leafy Greens — Lettuce, Spinach, and Amaranthaceae

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
```
LETTUCE (Lactuca sativa) — ASTERACEAE:
  Most consumed leafy vegetable globally by volume (~27 million tonnes/yr)
  Origin: Egypt/Mediterranean; ancestor Lactuca serriola (prickly lettuce)
  Domestication: elongated, non-bitter forms selected; 4,500+ years of cultivation
  Wild Lactuca: contains lactucin and lactucopicrin (bitter sesquiterpene lactones)
    → selected for reduced bitterness; still present in outer/older leaves
    → Lactuca genus name: from lac (milk) — milky latex in cut stems

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
TYPES:
    Crisphead (iceberg): tight ball; crisp water-rich leaves; lowest nutrient density
    Romaine/cos: upright; good nutrient retention; Ceasar salad base
    Butterhead (Boston, Bibb): soft loose head; mild flavor
    Loose-leaf: continuous harvest; red-leaf, green-leaf; nutritionally richest
    Batavia/oakleaf: European styles; serrated margins

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
BOLTING: when temperature + photoperiod triggers flowering, lettuce turns bitter fast
    → gibberellin signaling → rapid stem elongation + bitter compound upregulation
    → commercial growers use day-length-insensitive (slow-bolt) varieties

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
SPINACH (Spinacia oleracea) — AMARANTHACEAE:
  Origin: Persia (Iran); arrived in Europe ~700 CE via Arab traders
  ~26 million tonnes/yr globally; China produces ~90% of world's spinach

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
KEY NUTRIENTS: folate, vitamin K1, iron, magnesium, lutein, zeaxanthin
  OXALATE CAVEAT: spinach contains oxalic acid (~1g/100g)
    → Binds mineral ions (Fe²⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) → forms insoluble oxalates in gut
    → Despite high iron content, bioavailability is low (~1-2% vs. meat iron 20-30%)
    → Popeye's spinach-iron connection is nutritionally misleading for this reason
    → Cooking reduces oxalate but doesn't eliminate it; pairing with vitamin C helps

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
FAMILY AMARANTHACEAE (includes spinach, chard, beet, quinoa, amaranth):
  Formerly Chenopodiaceae; merged by molecular phylogenetics
  Distinctive: C3/C4 mixed family; many desert and salt-tolerant species
  Betalains (not anthocyanins): red/yellow pigments in beet, chard; missing from rest
    of plant kingdom — only Caryophyllales have betalains (cannot co-occur with anthocyanins)

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
SWISS CHARD (Beta vulgaris ssp. cicla):
  Same species as red beet and sugar beet (different organ selected: leaf vs. root vs. root+sugar)
  Colorful stems: betalain pigments (yellow: betaxanthins; red: betacyanins)
  Tolerates heat better than spinach → summer alternative
  Oxalate content similar to spinach; same mineral-binding caveat applies
```

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Vegetables - Brassica, Solanaceae, Allium, and the Domestication of Diversity

sections.text:
| If you need to diagnose... | Start With | Key Caveat |
|----------------------------|------------|------------|
| Brassica diversity | Which organ was selected | Cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, and kohlrabi are one species |
| Broccoli health claim | Glucosinolate -> myrosinase -> isothiocyanate chemistry | Preparation changes sulforaphane availability |
| Nightshade fear | Solanaceae alkaloids | Tomato/potato fear was overbroad but not irrational |
| Garlic pungency | Alliinase and alliin compartmentalization | Raw, cooked, powdered, and black garlic have different active compounds |
| Onion tears | Lachrymatory-factor gas from damaged cells | Chilling slows enzymes; goggles beat folklore |
| Cucurbit origin claim | Species-level domestication, not culinary category | Squash, melon, cucumber, and gourd histories differ |
| Leafy-green nutrition claim | Oxalate, bioavailability, and preparation | High mineral content is not the same as absorbed mineral |
